title: The hill at Uhud
hookLine: the archers leave the hill, the battle turns, and the Prophet ﷺ is wounded

cards: A year after Badr, Mecca comes back, and this time it's ready. Three thousand men march on Medina.
The Muslims, about seven hundred after a group turns back, meet them at the foot of a mountain just north of the city: Uhud. Beside the battlefield is a small hill.
The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ puts fifty archers on it, under a companion named 'Abdullah ibn Jubayr, to guard the Muslims' back from the enemy's horsemen. His order is hard to misread.
Sahih al-Bukhari keeps it: even if you see birds snatching us up, don't leave your place until I send for you.

teach.b: At first the battle goes the Muslims' way. The Meccan lines break, and their camp is left open, full of goods.
Up on the hill, the archers watch their friends below gathering the spoils, and start saying: it's over, we've won, let's go down. 'Abdullah ibn Jubayr reminds them of the order. Most go anyway.
He stays, with fewer than ten. Watching from the Meccan side is a cavalry commander, Khalid ibn al-Walid.
He sees the hill empty, circles behind it, and charges into the Muslims' backs. Everything turns. The men left on the hill are killed.

The Prophet himself is struck: Sahih Muslim says his tooth was broken and his face was cut, and he wiped away the blood. Word spreads that he's been killed, and some fighters drop their swords and sit down.
Later the Qur'an speaks to them directly, without flattery.
God kept his promise to you, it says, until you lost heart, and quarreled over the order, and disobeyed, after he'd shown you what you loved. Some of you wanted this world.

And to those who panicked at the rumor: Muhammad is only a messenger, and messengers have passed away before him. Will you turn back on your heels? And then, remarkably, it says God has forgiven them.

The lesson Muslims draw is simple and hard: hold the post you were given, even when the job looks done. This week in a line: an ummah, a call, a turning, a fast, a victory, a mercy, and now a hill left too soon.

how: Pilgrims to Medina visit Mount Uhud and the small archers' hill beside it, often called Jabal ar-Rumah, and Muslim teachers tell the story as a lesson in obedience and staying at one's post.

o: the hill near Mecca where pilgrims stand and pray
a fortress the Meccans built to guard their city
the mountain by Medina where the battle turned

games.q: what's inside the story — tap the pairs.

s: all fifty archers left the hill
'Abdullah ibn Jubayr stayed with fewer than ten, and they were killed.
the Prophet was wounded at Uhud
Sahih Muslim says his tooth was broken and his face was cut.
the Qur'an praises the archers at Uhud
it says they lost heart, quarreled and disobeyed, and then that God forgave them.

games.q: you're an archer on the hill. below, the enemy is running and your friends are gathering the spoils. what do you do?
o: send one archer down to check.
games.why: most went down. the few who stayed were killed, Khalid charged through the gap, and the battle turned.

practice: Ask yourself what your hill is: the thing you've been trusted with that's easy to walk away from once it looks finished, a promise to a friend, a shift at work, a child's homework, a habit you started on this path.
Picture the moment you're most likely to leave it early, when it seems nobody would notice, and then picture yourself staying.

wordCard.voice: Uhud, the mountain just north of Medina where fifty archers were told never to leave a hill, and most left, and the battle turned.

orig.note: Arabic: Uhud, the mountain just north of Medina.

carryVoice: Your line: hold the hill. Fewer than ten stayed when the rest went down. A week ends here.
